lead: Operating companies, health systems, and the largest medtech and biopharma acquirers are carrying 2026 deal activity, and operating companies are winning auctions against sponsors while senior debt prices at 7.8%. Private equity’s healthcare services count, by contrast, is tracking to its lowest year since 2017.

The policy calendar weighs on valuations as much as financing does: Medicaid redeterminations begin in January, so a Medicaid-weighted provider should expect diligence on enrollment attrition, and negotiated Medicare drug prices cut Guardian Pharmacy’s growth to 2% in one quarter.

points.b: Private equity completed an estimated 337 healthcare services transactions in the first half of 2026, a pace of 674 for the year and the lowest annual count since 2017 (PitchBook via Fierce Healthcare).

Medtech deal value reached $36.5 billion in the first half (PwC via MedTech Dive), biopharma deal value reached $130 billion in six months, almost matching all of 2025 (IQVIA), and hospitals and health systems announced 56 transactions through September, 16 of them in the third quarter (Kaufman Hall).

Medicare has proposed 2027 physician conversion factors of $33.17 and $32.84, reductions of 1.19% and 1.68%, while outpatient, surgery center, and home health rates are proposed to rise 2.4% and Medicare Advantage rates rise 2.48% (CMS). Medicaid work requirements and six-month eligibility reviews for expansion adults begin in January 2027 (CMS).

The Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75% to 4.00% on September 16, and the 10-year Treasury yielded 5.09% on October 16 (Federal Reserve; US Treasury). In a small sample of buyout loans, direct-lender spreads averaged 509 basis points in the second quarter against 474 in the first (PitchBook).

Private equity paid a median 13.6x EBITDA for healthcare services companies in 2025, on median target revenue of $162.5 million (PitchBook via Becker’s ASC Review), while completed Middle Market transactions across industries averaged 7.0x (GF Data via ACG) and 87% of sales above $5 million drew three or more offers (IBBA and M&A Source).

National health spending grew 6.8% in the year to July 2026 to 18.4% of GDP (Altarum), and CMS projects nearly $9.0 trillion by 2034 (CMS). California now requires transaction notices from private equity groups and management services organizations, and Maine’s 180-day notice and approval regime begins January 1, 2027 (Nixon Peabody; Foley & Lardner).

lead: US national health expenditures have risen in every year of the series, from $3.3 trillion in 2016 to $5.3 trillion in 2024, or 18.0% of GDP, and CMS projects $5.7 trillion for 2025 and $6.0 trillion for 2026 (CMS). Hospital and health system transaction counts have been far less steady, moving with financing costs and policy: they fell to a series low in 2025 and have since recovered, with the first three quarters of 2026 already ahead of the full prior year (Kaufman Hall).

points.b: CMS projects average annual health spending growth of 5.4% from 2025 to 2034, against 4.1% for the economy, which would take national health expenditures to $9.0 trillion (Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget).
Announced hospital and health system transactions fell from 117 in 2017 to 49 in 2021, recovered to 72 in 2024, and then dropped to 46 in 2025, the fewest in the series (Kaufman Hall).

The first three quarters of 2026 produced 56 announced hospital transactions, with 22 in the first quarter, 18 in the second, and 16 in the third, so the year has already passed the 2025 total (Kaufman Hall).

Private equity completed 1,217 healthcare services transactions in 2021 and an estimated 747 in 2025, which leaves sponsor activity well below its earlier level even before the 2026 slowdown (PitchBook).

lead: Healthcare employment, facility construction, and novel drug approvals all stand above their 2021 levels, which supports demand in provider services, life sciences and diagnostics, medical products and distribution, and pharmacy and healthcare services. The constraints have moved to labor and capital budgets: clinician supply is tight enough that buyers test turnover as closely as payer mix, and hospital executives planning capital cuts shift spending from new construction toward acquisition.

points.b: Healthcare employed 18.55 million people in September 2026, 16.1% more than in September 2021 and 2.0% more than a year earlier, with the monthly series rising from 16.0 million and pausing only briefly in early 2026 (Bureau of Labor Statistics via FRED).

Health care and social assistance had 1,359,000 open positions in August (Bureau of Labor Statistics JOLTS), and buyers now test clinician turnover as closely as payer mix when they assess a provider.

Healthcare construction ran at an annual rate of $75.8 billion in August 2026, 49% above September 2021 in nominal dollars, after peaking at $79 billion in April 2025 and easing to $74 billion in early 2026 (US Census Bureau via FRED).
Among hospital and health system executives surveyed, 41% plan to cut capital spending in 2026 (Sage Growth Partners via HFMA), which shifts spending from new construction toward acquisition.
The FDA approved 46 novel drugs in 2025 and 46 in 2026 through October 9, against a low of 37 in 2022 and a high of 59 in 2018 (FDA; RAPS).
Outsourced research has recovered alongside approvals, with IQVIA booking $1.22 of new work for each dollar of revenue in the second quarter (IQVIA).

lead: Sponsor volume in healthcare services has run a full cycle since 2017: steady platform building, a 2021 peak, three years of decline as the Medicare physician conversion factor fell, a partial recovery in 2025, and a 2026 pace that is the lowest since 2017. Physician practice deals are down 46% on pace, while hospitals and other strategic buyers have kept transaction activity going (PitchBook; Kaufman Hall).

points.b: From 2017 to 2019, private equity completed between 490 and 684 healthcare services transactions a year, while hospitals announced 117 transactions in 2017 and 92 in 2019 (PitchBook; Kaufman Hall).
Volume rose to 829 in 2020 and then to 1,217 in 2021, the highest annual count in the PitchBook series and the reference point against which the later decline is measured (PitchBook).
Annual volume fell from 998 in 2022 to 682 in 2024, while the Medicare conversion factor fell from $34.61 in 2022 to $32.35 in 2025 before rising to $33.40 in 2026 (AMA).

Volume recovered to an estimated 747 in 2025, but the first half of 2026 produced an estimated 337, with physician practice deals down 46% on pace (PitchBook), while hospitals announced 56 transactions through September (Kaufman Hall).
The 2026 figure of 674 annualizes the first-half estimate, the 2025 count is itself an estimate, and PitchBook restates earlier years as late-reported transactions are added (PitchBook).

lead: Operating companies and the largest platforms are buying through 7.8% senior debt and 500-basis-point spreads because they pay from cash flow, while private equity’s healthcare services count runs at a 2017 pace. Benchmark International expects that division to hold through the first half of 2027, with sponsor volume returning once the September rate increase is absorbed and the 2027 Medicare and Medicaid rules are final.

For an owner, the next twelve months favor a process built around strategic buyers, launched with the payer-mix and enrollment analysis already done and timed ahead of the sponsor exits that will crowd the second half of 2027.

points.b: Operating companies bought seven of the nine named sellers in Benchmark International’s last 24 months of healthcare closings, HCA has added about 70 urgent care centers this year, and Danaher, Merck KGaA, and Labcorp are paying for consumables and testing volume. A buyer list that leads with strategics and brings in sponsors for competitive tension suits a 2027 process.

The 2027 physician fee schedule proposes conversion factor cuts of 1.2% to 1.7%, Medicaid work requirements and six-month redeterminations start in January, and laboratory fee cuts of up to 15% a year resume unless the RESULTS Act passes. An owner who brings a line-by-line analysis of these items to the first meeting stays in control of the valuation conversation.

The listed reference set trades at 14.3x adjusted EBITDA, with provider services at 14.2x, medical products at 10.7x, pharmacy services at 15.0x, and life sciences and diagnostics re-rated to 18.7x. Private healthcare services deals cleared a 13.6x median in 2025 against 5.8x for $5 million to $50 million businesses, a gap explained by scale, contracted revenue, and payer mix.

PitchBook’s healthcare analyst expects mean reversion from the 2026 low, and AMN and Thermo Fisher both described fuller pipelines on their second-quarter calls. Sponsor exits are running 26% below last year’s pace, which builds a backlog of platforms waiting to sell, and owners who launch in the first half of 2027 meet buyers before that backlog clears.

Integer shareholders vote on the KKR offer and the FOMC meets in late October; final CY2027 physician fee schedule, outpatient, and home health rules follow; January 1, 2027 brings Medicaid work requirements, Maine’s 180-day notice regime, and PAMA lab cuts absent legislation; and mid-January full-year counts from Kaufman Hall and PitchBook set the 2026 baseline.

lead: Buyer sets and demand drivers differ across the four sectors. In provider services, health systems are buying access points and sponsors are trading platforms; in life sciences and diagnostics, research spending has turned up and laboratories are selling to the national networks; in medical products and distribution, procedure demand is firm and consumables are outgrowing capital equipment; and in pharmacy and healthcare services, drug pricing reform is reshaping pharmacy while staffing returns to growth.

points.b: The 100 largest urgent care operators hold 6,056 of the country’s 14,655 centers, and 55.9% of those locations are affiliated with a hospital (Journal of Urgent Care Medicine). HCA Healthcare acquired about 70 centers in three 2026 transactions: CommunityMed, Urgent Care Group, and Texas MedClinic (Becker’s ASC Review; Healthcare Dive).

General Atlantic bought TEAM Services Group at about $3 billion (LevinPro), and Kinderhook agreed to take Enhabit private at about $1.1 billion (Enhabit). Independent practice continues to shrink, with 42.2% of physicians in physician-owned practices against 60.1% in 2012 (AMA via Medical Economics).

Quest grew revenue 10.2% in the second quarter on 13.1% more requisitions (Quest Diagnostics), and Labcorp agreed acquisitions with total consideration of $528.6 million in the first half (Labcorp Form 10-Q). Medicare laboratory fee cuts of up to 15% a year could resume in 2027 unless Congress passes the RESULTS Act (ADLM).

IQVIA’s net bookings rose 19% (IQVIA) and Medpace grew revenue 17.2% (Medpace), while sponsor-backed networks such as Headlands Research and Summit Clinical Research continue to buy clinical research sites, and Thermo Fisher, Danaher, Agilent, and Merck KGaA buy in tools and reagents.

Stryker grew 9.0% organically in the second quarter, and Steris grew healthcare consumables 9% against 1% for capital equipment (Stryker; Steris). Platinum Equity agreed to buy Owens & Minor’s products business, and Apollo bought a 13% interest in McKesson’s medical-surgical unit for $1.25 billion (Owens & Minor; McKesson).

US net medicine spending reached $606 billion in 2025, up 10.6% (IQVIA Institute), yet negotiated Medicare prices held Guardian’s revenue growth to 2% while it served 8% more residents (Guardian Pharmacy Services). BrightSpring’s pharmacy solutions revenue grew 22% to $3.4 billion, and healthcare staffing is forecast to grow 1% to $39.0 billion in 2026 (BrightSpring; Staffing Industry Analysts).

lead: Buyers of founder-owned healthcare businesses fall into two groups in each sector: the listed reference companies used in the valuation sections, and the private platforms, sponsors, health systems, and strategic buyers named in 2026 transactions. HCA Healthcare appears in both groups in provider services, and the private buyer lists mix financial sponsors such as KKR, Apollo, and Knox Lane with operating companies such as Merck KGaA, Medline, and Leica Biosystems.

points.b: The listed reference companies are HCA Healthcare, Tenet Health, U.S. Physical Therapy, DaVita Kidney Care, Addus HomeCare, Pennant Group, Acadia Healthcare, LifeStance Health, Privia Health, Concentra, and Ensign Group. Private buyers include HCA Healthcare, MyEyeDr., EyeCare Partners, Kinderhook Industries, Universal Health Services, ACES, MKH Capital Partners, Grant Avenue Capital, and Global Medical Response.

The listed reference companies are Labcorp, Quest Diagnostics, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Danaher, Bio-Techne, IQVIA, Medpace, ICON, and Charles River Laboratories. Research networks and strategic buyers include Headlands Research, Summit Clinical Research, Worldwide Clinical Trials, Fortrea, Resonetics, Agilent Technologies, Merck KGaA, and Leica Biosystems.

The listed reference companies are Stryker, Steris, Teleflex, Henry Schein, Dentsply Sirona, Envista, Zimmer Biomet, Integer Holdings, Solventum, and Viemed Healthcare. Sponsors and product strategics include Mitsui Chemicals, Aspen Surgical, KKR, Platinum Equity, Hanger, Apollo, Medline, Intersurgical, and Montagu and Kohlberg.

The listed reference companies are Option Care Health, BrightSpring Health Services, Guardian Pharmacy Services, McKesson, Cencora, Cardinal Health, CVS Health, and AMN Healthcare. Pharmacy, staffing, and logistics buyers include Knox Lane, JLL Partners, Soleo Health, GenieRx Holdings, Strata Critical Medical, VeloSource (Interlock Equity), Care Career, and Elite365 Family of Brands.

lead: The six transactions span all four sectors and show the main routes to a sale this year: a strategic buyer paying a premium for recurring consumable demand, a listed operator buying personal care scale at about one times revenue, a sponsor-built pathology roll-up sold to a strategic, a take-private of a contract manufacturer, and two sales whose terms were shaped by the seller’s balance sheet or by antitrust review. Benchmark International did not advise on these transactions.

points.b: MyEyeDr. agreed in September to buy the optometry business of EyeCare Partners, with more than 300 offices, and EyeCare Partners will apply the proceeds to debt reduction (Eyewire News; EyeCare Partners). A sponsor-backed platform sold a division to a competitor to repair its balance sheet, and the consolidator with capacity set the terms.

Addus HomeCare will pay about $275 million for AccentCare’s personal care operations outside New York, which have about $280 million of annual revenue in ten states (Addus HomeCare). About one times revenue, paid in cash by a listed operator, is the current reference for personal care scale.

Merck KGaA agreed in June to acquire Bio-Techne at an enterprise value of $11.3 billion, with closing expected by early 2027 (Bio-Techne). The strategic paid a 36% premium for reagents and instruments with recurring consumable demand.

Leica Biosystems bought StatLab, a maker of anatomic pathology consumables with about $250 million of 2025 revenue, from Audax and Linden, closing on September 28 (Danaher; PE Professional). Its sponsors built it through nine add-on acquisitions in five years, a path open to other pathology suppliers.

KKR agreed in August to take Integer Holdings private at $127 a share, an enterprise value of $5.7 billion and a 51.8% premium to the undisturbed price, with closing expected by year end (Integer; Medical Design & Outsourcing). A 52% premium for contract device manufacturing supports demand for smaller manufacturers as add-ons.

Knox Lane completed its $437 million purchase of Cross Country Healthcare at $13.25 a share on July 21, after Aya Healthcare ended an agreement at $18.61 following an extended FTC review (Fierce Healthcare; Staffing Industry Analysts). The delay cost the seller $5.36 a share, so antitrust timing belongs in process design for mergers of scale.

lead: Benchmark International advised the seller on twelve transactions that closed in provider services, life sciences and diagnostics, medical products and distribution, and pharmacy and healthcare services over the trailing 24 months, nine of which are shown. The buyer mix matches the wider healthcare market described in the report: operating companies acquired seven of the nine sellers shown, and financial buyers acquired the other two.

points.b: Four of the nine sellers shown are life sciences and diagnostics companies, three are in pharmacy and healthcare services, and one each comes from provider services and from medical products and distribution.

Seven of the nine sellers shown were bought by an operating company, one by a private equity firm, and one by a group of private investors, consistent with strategic buyers setting the pace in healthcare.

The sellers are specialized businesses with a defined service or product niche, including clinical and executive staffing, testing and certification, contract manufacturing, dental devices, and in-home care for Medicaid waiver participants.
Benchmark International is the world’s #1 privately owned sell-side M&A advisor, based on PitchBook’s Q2 2026 Global League Tables (Benchmark International).

lead: Re-rating in tools and reagents and in research services added 5.4 turns to the life sciences and diagnostics median, the only large move among the four sectors, while provider services, medical products and distribution, and pharmacy and healthcare services stayed close to last year’s levels. Private-market reference points sit below most listed medians, because listed companies are many times larger than a founder-owned business and a private company’s price is set by its own earnings, growth, and risk.

points.b: Median EV to trailing adjusted EBITDA moved from 14.5x to 14.2x in provider services, 13.3x to 18.7x in life sciences and diagnostics, 12.0x to 10.7x in medical products and distribution, and 14.2x to 15.0x in pharmacy and healthcare services (company filings; StockAnalysis).

Tools and reagents rose from 19.5x to 25.0x and research services from 11.1x to 16.8x, while clinical laboratories moved only from 13.3x to 13.5x; Bio-Techne trades at its agreed acquisition price (company filings; StockAnalysis).

Hospitals, behavioral, and post-acute operators rose from 8.6x to 9.2x while outpatient, physician, and home care fell from 18.8x to 17.1x; devices, consumables, and manufacturing rose from 12.6x to 14.3x, and dental, distribution, and home equipment fell from 9.6x to 8.0x.

Pharmacy services and staffing rose from 14.3x to 15.8x, and drug distribution and retail rose from 14.2x to 15.0x, measured on enterprise value at October 16, 2026 against September 30, 2025 (company filings; StockAnalysis).

Private equity paid a median 13.6x EBITDA for healthcare services companies in 2025 on median target revenue of $162.5 million (PitchBook via Becker’s ASC Review), against a 7.0x average for completed Middle Market transactions (GF Data via ACG) and 5.8x for $5 million to $50 million businesses (IBBA and M&A Source) in the second quarter of 2026.

lead: Shares rose over the 52 weeks to October 16, 2026 at 29 of the 38 listed reference companies, and pharmacy and healthcare services led, with every company in the sector higher. Medical products lagged, with six of ten companies up, the smallest median gain, and a median price at 86% of the 52-week high, the lowest of the four sectors (StockAnalysis).

points.b: Median 52-week share price changes, excluding dividends, were +21.5% for provider services, +21.8% for life sciences and diagnostics, +12.1% for medical products, and +44.3% for pharmacy and healthcare services (StockAnalysis).
Median share prices stand at 93% of the 52-week high in life sciences and diagnostics, 88% in pharmacy and healthcare services, 87% in provider services, and 86% in medical products (StockAnalysis).

LifeStance Health rose 126.2%, AMN Healthcare 111.0%, and BrightSpring Health Services 108.4%, followed by Concentra at 85.7%, Charles River Laboratories at 75.8%, Pennant Group at 72.9%, and Cardinal Health at 63.2% (StockAnalysis).

Dentsply Sirona fell 33.0% and Stryker 20.3%, with smaller declines at Privia Health, ICON, Steris, U.S. Physical Therapy, Zimmer Biomet, and Ensign Group, while Addus HomeCare was unchanged at 0.0% (StockAnalysis).

Shares rose at 7 of 11 provider companies, 8 of 9 life sciences and diagnostics companies, 6 of 10 medical products companies, and 8 of 8 pharmacy and healthcare services companies; Bio-Techne and Integer Holdings trade near agreed acquisition prices (StockAnalysis).

lead: Growth, margins, and multiples rank the four sectors differently. Provider companies lead on growth, with 14.0% median trailing revenue growth and 8.7% expected for the current fiscal year, while life sciences and diagnostics combines the highest adjusted EBITDA margin, the highest free cash flow margin, and the highest revenue and EBITDA multiples. Pharmacy and healthcare services posts a 4.9% median EBITDA margin, held down by drug distribution, yet trades at 15.0x EBITDA, second only to life sciences (company filings; StockAnalysis).

points.b: Median trailing twelve-month revenue growth, including acquisitions, was 14.0% for provider services, 9.6% for pharmacy and healthcare services, 8.4% for medical products, and 6.4% for life sciences and diagnostics (company filings; StockAnalysis).

Analysts expect median current-year growth of 8.7% for provider services, 6.8% for life sciences and diagnostics, 5.6% for medical products, and 4.7% for pharmacy and healthcare services; life sciences is the only sector whose consensus exceeds its trailing rate, although fiscal years differ (StockAnalysis).

Median adjusted EBITDA margins are 22.9% in life sciences and diagnostics, 22.3% in medical products, 13.1% in provider services, and 4.9% in pharmacy and healthcare services, and free cash flow margins follow the same order at 12.9%, 9.2%, 8.0%, and 2.8%.

Median enterprise value to trailing revenue is 4.3x in life sciences and diagnostics, 2.7x in medical products, 1.8x in provider services, and 0.5x in pharmacy and healthcare services (StockAnalysis).

Median EV to trailing adjusted EBITDA is 18.7x for life sciences and diagnostics, 15.0x for pharmacy and healthcare services, 14.2x for provider services, and 10.7x for medical products, against 13.3x, 14.2x, 14.5x, and 12.0x a year ago for the same companies.

lead: Results for quarters ended June 2026 put skilled nursing and research services at the top, with Ensign Group growing revenue 17.3% and Medpace 17.2%, while Thermo Fisher Scientific, Quest Diagnostics, Stryker, and Labcorp grew between 5.8% and 10.5%, and AMN Healthcare, Guardian Pharmacy Services, and Option Care Health grew about 2%. Management commentary in all four sectors describes more assets coming to market and active acquisition pipelines (earnings releases).

points.b: HCA Healthcare and IQVIA each grew revenue 8.7%, U.S. Physical Therapy 8.5%, Addus HomeCare 8.0%, McKesson 7.7%, Steris 7.3%, Tenet Healthcare 6.8%, Henry Schein 6.7%, and Cardinal Health 5.8%, all including acquisitions (earnings releases).

Chad Keetch, Chief Investment Officer of The Ensign Group, sees opportunities from larger portfolios, landlords replacing tenants, and non-profits divesting post-acute assets, while Addus HomeCare’s Dirk Allison reports more personal care opportunities and more optimism about skilled home health deals since the 2027 proposed rate.

Quest Diagnostics’ Jim Davis describes hospitals under workforce and financial pressure turning to Quest as a strategic partner, and Thermo Fisher’s Marc Casper says capital deployment continues to prioritize strategic M&A, with an active pipeline in a highly fragmented industry.

STERIS CEO Dan Carestio expects tariffs to drive localization in the US and Europe, with some duplication of manufacturing sites, and Henry Schein’s Fred Lowery expects consolidation among dental service organizations, driven by the Middle Market, to let the company outgrow the broader dental market.

Cardinal Health CEO Jason Hollar points to fast-growing categories in urology, oncology, and neurology, and AMN Healthcare CFO and COO Brian Scott says that after a relatively quiet year, more assets have come to market over the last couple of quarters.

lead: The appendix sets out market capitalization, enterprise value, share price performance, growth, margins, and multiples for each of the 38 listed reference companies as of October 16, 2026, grouped by sector and subsector. Across the full set the median company trades at 14.3x trailing adjusted EBITDA and 1.91x revenue, on 8.4% revenue growth and a 17.2% adjusted EBITDA margin (company filings; StockAnalysis).

points.b: Hospital, behavioral, and post-acute operators such as HCA Healthcare at 9.5x, DaVita at 8.6x, and Tenet Healthcare at 6.9x trade well below outpatient and home-based peers such as LifeStance Health at 22.9x and Pennant Group at 22.6x; the sector median is 14.2x on 14.0% growth.

Research services and tools companies carry the highest multiples in the set, led by Medpace at 27.6x, Bio-Techne at 26.4x, Thermo Fisher Scientific at 25.0x, and Danaher at 23.1x, while Labcorp and Quest Diagnostics trade at 13.0x and 14.0x; the sector median is 18.7x.

Stryker trades at 17.2x and Teleflex at 15.5x, while Dentsply Sirona at 6.1x and Viemed Healthcare at 5.8x sit at the low end; Dentsply Sirona is also at 58% of its 52-week high, the lowest in the set, and the sector median is 10.7x.

Drug distributors McKesson, Cencora, and Cardinal Health earn adjusted EBITDA margins of 1.5% to 1.7% yet trade at 14.9x to 17.3x EBITDA, while BrightSpring at 20.1x and Guardian Pharmacy Services at 19.4x lead pharmacy services and AMN Healthcare trades at 5.7x.

LTM covers the twelve months to June 30, 2026, a year-ago multiple uses enterprise value at September 30, 2025, and depreciation is added where a company reports adjusted operating income; Teleflex has no comparable year-ago figure.

lead: Four third-quarter pieces, one for each sector, cover the slowdown in sponsor-backed healthcare services transactions, first-half medtech and biopharma acquisitions, and pharmacy consolidation, each paired with a marked passage and the takeaway for an owner. Read together, they describe large strategic buyers spending heavily while sponsor deal counts and retail pharmacy numbers fall.

points.b: Fierce Healthcare (August 19, 2026) reports PitchBook’s finding that private equity is on pace for 674 healthcare services transactions in 2026 after an estimated 337 in the first half, and PitchBook’s Brian Wright expects mean reversion toward the longer-run level.

MedTech Dive (July 6, 2026) reports PwC’s count of $36.5 billion of medtech acquisitions in the first half, led by Boston Scientific’s $14.5 billion purchase of Penumbra and Danaher’s $9.9 billion purchase of Masimo.

IQVIA (July 8, 2026) finds biopharma deal value of $130 billion in six months, almost matching 2025, across 42 deals of $250 million or more; spending by these large buyers supports demand for the research, laboratory, and manufacturing services that founder-owned companies supply.

Drug Channels (August 11, 2026) reports almost 8,000 fewer retail pharmacies than in 2018 and more than 2,000 closures in 2025, while dispensing revenues reached a record $751 billion, up 10%; scale, specialty mix, and payer contracts decide which pharmacies remain attractive to a buyer.
